nameStory: The Red Knot gets its name from the stunning rusty-red plumage it sports during breeding season, particularly on its breast and face. The word 'knot' comes from the Old English 'cnotta,' possibly referring to the bird's compact, rounded build when it hunches against coastal winds.
description: The Red Knot is a chunky, medium-sized sandpiper about the size of a robin that visits New England's coastlines during migration. In spring, these birds show off gorgeous brick-red breeding plumage on their chest and face, while in fall they wear more subdued gray-brown feathers. They have sturdy, straight black bills perfect for probing sand and a stocky build that makes them look robust compared to other sandpipers.

idTips.label: Stocky Build
idTips.description: Noticeably chunky and robust compared to other sandpipers, with a thick neck and rounded body that gives it a sturdy, almost football-like appearance

idTips.label: Straight Bill
idTips.description: Medium-length black bill that's perfectly straight and sturdy-looking, about as long as the head and blunt at the tip

idTips.label: Rusty-Red Breeding Plumage
idTips.description: In spring, displays rich brick-red coloring on the face, throat, and breast that looks almost rusty or cinnamon-colored in good light

idTips.label: Gray Winter Plumage
idTips.description: In fall and winter, wears plain gray-brown upperparts with a clean white belly and subtle pale eyebrow stripe

idTips.label: Greenish-Yellow Legs
idTips.description: Short, sturdy legs that are typically dull yellow-green or olive colored, never bright yellow or black

idTips.label: Flocking Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen in tight, coordinated flocks that wheel and turn together like a living cloud, especially during migration

habitat: Red Knots visit New England's sandy beaches, mudflats, and rocky shorelines during spring and fall migration. Look for them on wide, open beaches with exposed sand or mud where they can probe for shellfish and marine worms. They're particularly fond of areas with good populations of small clams and other mollusks.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration in May brings birds in brilliant rusty-red breeding plumage. They're often feeding frantically to fuel up for their journey to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Very few remain in New England during summer, as most are on Arctic tundra breeding grounds. Any spotted are likely non-breeding individuals.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration from August through October shows birds in plain gray winter plumage. Juveniles have a scaly pattern on their backs.
seasonality.winter: Rare in winter, as most continue south to warmer coastal areas. Any winter sightings are notable and worth reporting to local birding groups.

funFact: Red Knots can smell buried clams through sand and actually time their migrations to arrive at beaches just when horseshoe crabs are laying eggs - they can double their body weight in just two weeks by gorging on these protein-rich eggs!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Dunlin, but Red Knots are noticeably chunkier with straighter bills and lack the Dunlin's curved bill tip. In breeding plumage, Dunlin have black belly patches while Red Knots are solidly rusty-red on the chest. Memory trick: Red Knots are 'thick' like a knot in rope, Dunlin are slim and 'done-lean.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Red' Knots, they only show red coloring during breeding season in spring. The rest of the year they're quite gray and plain, which often surprises beginning birders expecting to see red birds year-round.
compareHints: Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper. While Purple Sandpiper is similarly stocky, it prefers rocky shores and has a slightly curved bill and different leg color. Red Knot's straight bill and preference for sandy beaches helps distinguish it from other medium-sized sandpipers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
